episodes.161337: A shortwave trough progressed across the region. As a result, scattered showers and thunderstorms developed across western Colorado. However, dry low levels led to gusty winds rather than heavy wetting rains with convection. Some storms generated severe wind gusts.
episodes.161401: Showers and thunderstorms repeatedly moved across Northern Madison and into Western Jackson Counties during the mid-morning hours, lingering into the afternoon hours on the 19th. Numerous flooding reports were received as 3-5 of rainfall occurred, resulting in 1 fatality in Northern Madison County.
episodes.161531: A large cluster of thunderstorms developed over Seminole County in the late afternoon due to colliding outflow boundaries. These thunderstorms were nearly stationary for several hours over northern Seminole County, where hourly rainfall rates of 2 to 4 inches occurred. Much of the Sanford and Lake Mary areas received between 4 and 6 inches of rain within 2 to 3 hours. | |Localized flash flooding occurred in the Sanford area of Seminole County. Numerous streets and sidewalks became impassable due to high standing water,  causing several cars to stall. Water briefly entered one home, several garages nearby, and flooded the property of several businesses in downtown Sanford.
episodes.162265: A saturated tropical airmass (PWAT over 2 inches) combined with diurnal instability and fueled locally heavy rainfall in showers and storms that formed near a meandering trough axis across north Florida and sea breezes. Weak storm motion enabled locally heavy rainfall to form and train over areas.
episodes.162267: A weak east-west oriented trough extended across NE Florida and served as a focus for localized heavy rainfall under a saturated airmass (PWAT over 2 inches). Slow storm motion and PVA in the afternoon enhanced heavy rainfall.
episodes.162382: The remnants of Hurricane Nicholas moved across the region. Numerous showers and thunderstorms produced flash flooding.
episodes.162530: A dry microburst from a virga shower passing over the Johnson County Airport in Buffalo produced strong wind gusts with a maximum gust of 63 mph.
episodes.162662: Slow moving thunderstorms resulted in flash flooding and a road washout in Geneva County.
episodes.163105: A tropical air mass covered Alabama on September 18-19 with precipitable water values over 2 inches. An nearly stationary upper low near the Texas and Louisiana state line provided lift and instability for showers and thunderstorms across the Central Gulf States. An inverted surface trough was located along the I-20 corridor on September 18th, and provided a focus for slow moving thunderstorms that produced flash flooding across Tuscaloosa, Jefferson and Shelby counties. The upper trough moved slightly eastward on the 19th and the flooding threat shifted to areas east of I-65.
episodes.163529: Showers and thunderstorms repeatedly moved across Northern Alabama and Southern Middle TN on the 19th and 20th. Numerous roads were closed in Lincoln County, with widespread rainfall amounts of 3-6 across much of the area. Portions of NW Madison received 6-8 over a few hours, leading to flash flooding.
episodes.163538: An isolated storm produced a waterspout south of Pensacola Beach.
episodes.163542: A warm front was lifting north of the state during the afternoon of the 19th, with high pressure located east of the state. The result was warm and moist return southeast flow across the state. Showers and thunderstorms developed just east of the state in the higher terrain by mid-afternoon, and gained enough strength that they were able to push northwest and over the mountains into southeast Kentucky. The strongest storm in this line/cluster moved in Harlan County, resulting in a strong wind gust that knocked down a tree. The line of storms continue to progress northwestward through eastern Kentucky during the early evening hours, eventually losing strength.
episodes.163553: Ridging over the eastern United States provided a weak east-northwest lower tropospheric flow over the Florida Keys, promoting strong island cloud line development.  An isolated waterspout developed in association with a convective rain shower west of Key West.

CoCoRaHS and mesonet reports indicated that between 4 and 6 inches of rain fell in just two to three hours during the late afternoon of September 19. Several observations over five inches were received from Sanford and Lake Mary (the highest value was from a Weather Underground mesonet site in Sanford; 5.90 inches). The ASOS at the Sanford International Airport (KSFB) measured 5.17 inches of rain, with 4.22 inches falling between 1600-1700 LST.
A 35 year old man drowned as a strong water current pulled him into a nearby drainage pipe along Bullard Road.

Between 4 and 6 inches of rain fell during the late afternoon hours in portions of northern Seminole County. Heavy thunderstorms that were nearly stationary produced significant rainfall accumulations in approximately 2 hours, and this resulted in localized flash flooding in the Sanford area. Standing water reached at least 2 feet in some spots, resulting in numerous road closure and several stalled vehicles. Flood waters briefly entered one home and several nearby garages. Several businesses in Downtown Sanford along 1st Street reported having 2-3 inches of water inside their establishments.
A water rescue was performed due to flash flooding on 7 M. Jones Road in Flintville.
